intro: You are standing on Aşıklı Höyük, a mound in Aksaray province whose story belongs to the 9th–8th millennium BC. This is a pre-pottery Neolithic mound near Aksaray, and from its soil have come the world's earliest domesticated sheep and buildings of moulded mudbrick. Shall we go back to the very beginnings of village life?
history: For about a millennium, between c. 8200 and 7500 BC, people lived here almost without a break. Since 1989 the mound has been excavated by Istanbul University, and what has come to light is remarkable: houses of moulded mudbrick, planned streets and the domestication of sheep. Together they make Aşıklı one of the earliest examples of settled life in Anatolia.
structure-1: Look at the moulded mudbrick houses. They were built from mudbrick blocks shaped in moulds, a building method that sets this mound apart. Imagine the builders turning out block after block, all of the same shape.
structure-2: Here are the ovens and hearths. This is where daily life happened: food was cooked over them, and they kept the houses warm. Pause for a moment and imagine the glow of the fire at the heart of each home.
structure-3: Now notice the regular street layout. This settlement was planned, with streets running parallel to one another. It is not a random cluster of huts, but a village laid out with intention.
structure-4: Next come the trash pits and burials. Burials and household pits may sound modest, but for archaeologists they are a treasure: they yield rich evidence of how people here lived their daily lives.
structure-5: Now picture the village-planned settlement as a whole. Its layout is arranged around communal spaces, just as is typical of early settlements. Here, life was organised around places that everyone used.
facts: Did you know? The earliest domesticated sheep bones found at Aşıklı are among the strongest pieces of evidence that sheep were domesticated in present-day Turkey. This is also the oldest known village in central Anatolia, from about 8400 BC, and it offers a step-by-step record of how farming arrived here. Perhaps the most moving find of all is a woman's skeleton bearing the trace of skull surgery, among the oldest evidence of brain surgery anywhere. She survived it, and lived on for some time afterwards.
outro: This brings our tour of Aşıklı Höyük to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. People made their homes on this mound for a very long time; let it keep its story for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
